newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia says normalisation with Serbia dragging.
newsitem.headline: Croatia says normalisation with Serbia dragging.

text.p: Croatia said on Friday the pace of normalisation in its relations with Yugoslavia, from which it seceded in 1991, was "too slow" but positive on the whole.

Croatia and Yugoslavia, which comprises Serbia and Montenegro, signed accords for full diplomatic relations on August 23 after a surprise summit between presidents Slobodan Milosevic of Serbia and Franjo Tudjman of Croatia.
The accords marked the end of a conflict that began after Croatia's independence from federal Yugoslavia, but left a host of bilateral problems to be solved in future talks.

"Normalisation of relations with Yugoslavia is not going at the expected pace in all areas (where agreements were reached)," the state news agency HINA quoted Croatian deputy Foreign Minister Hido Biscevic as saying.

Among possible reasons, he cited political turmoil in Yugoslavia where hundreds of thousands of demonstrators have been protesting for a month over the ruling Socialist Party's annulment of local election results.
Yugoslav Foreign Minister Milan Milutinovic made his first official visit to Zagreb in October.

His Croatian counterpart, Mate Granic, was to visit Belgrade in December for final talks on welfare, health and pension insurance, and co-operation of police. The disputed Prevlaka peninsula, on Croatia's southern Adriatic border with Montenegro, was expected to be tackled as well.
But Biscevic said Granic would not travel to Yugoslavia this year after all.

"Ministerial meetings usually come after there has been progress in the implementation of previous agreements," Biscevic said. "Expert teams from various fields need more time to complete their tasks."
But he said the normalisation process was "in principle positive, without major disputes or tensions".

Among other unresolved issues, he mentioned the Adriatic pipeline, supposed to supply crude oil to Serbia and Eastern Europe, air traffic which has been grounded since 1991, and the lack of a mutual payments system.
